rules.statement: Most verbs have six inflectional forms: three primary (preterite, 3rd singular present, plain present) and three secondary (plain form, gerund-participle, past participle).
rules.condition: Applies to the inflectional paradigm of an ordinary (non-be) verb lexeme: primary forms are preterite, 3rd person singular present tense and plain present tense; secondary forms are the plain form, the gerund-participle and the past participle.

correct.text: I need to write it. [plain form]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Auxiliary verbs also have negative forms (isn't, can't), noted on p. 50.

rules.statement: The verb be has two preterite forms (was, were) and three present forms (am, is, are); irrealis 'were' is a residual mood form found only with be and a 1st or 3rd person singular subject.
rules.condition: Applies to the verb be: preterite was/were, present am/is/are; irrealis mood 'were' (as in 'I wish she were here') occurs only with be with a 1st or 3rd person singular subject.

correct.text: I wish she were here. [irrealis were]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Descriptive classification only; the conditions under which irrealis 'were' is required or optional are not given here.

rules.statement: The plain form of a verb occurs in four constructions: imperative, subjunctive, TO-infinitival and bare infinitival; these are clause constructions, not inflectional forms, and 'to' is a VP subordinator.
rules.condition: Applies to clauses whose head is a plain-form verb: imperative (Take care!), subjunctive (essential that he take care), TO-infinitival (I advise you to take care) and bare infinitival (You must take care); imperative, subjunctive and infinitival are clause types, not verb forms.

correct.text: It is vital that she take care.
I want her to take care.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Cambridge treats these as clause constructions rather than verb inflections; Burton-Roberts's handling not checked.

rules.statement: Finite and non-finite are properties of clauses (and VPs), not of verb inflection: finite clauses are headed by a primary form or by a plain form in an imperative or subjunctive; non-finite clauses by a gerund-participle, past participle or infinitival plain form.
rules.condition: Applies when classifying a clause by the form of its head verb: finite if the head is a primary form or a plain form used in the imperative or subjunctive construction; non-finite if the head is a gerund-participle, a past participle or a plain form used in the infinitival construction.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: Auxiliary verbs are heads, not dependents: in 'She is writing a novel', 'is' is the head and 'writing a novel' is its complement, so 'is writing' is not a constituent.
rules.condition: Applies to the constituent structure of clauses with an auxiliary verb followed by a non-finite verb: the auxiliary is head of the clause, the non-finite clause is its complement, and the structure parallels 'She began writing a novel'.

correct.text: She is writing a novel. [is = head; writing a novel = complement]
She began writing a novel. [same structure]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Cambridge says its head analysis 'departs radically' from traditional grammar; Burton-Roberts's analysis not checked. Flag for comparison.

rules.review_notes: Possible cross-framework conflict; check against Burton-Roberts before engine use.

rules.concept: auxiliary vs lexical verbs: not and inversion
rules.statement: Auxiliary verbs can be negated by a following 'not' and can invert with the subject in interrogatives; lexical verbs cannot, and need the dummy auxiliary do instead.
rules.condition: Applies to a clause whose verb is a lexical (non-auxiliary) verb in a construction requiring negation with 'not' or subject-verb inversion: the lexical verb cannot itself be followed by 'not' or placed before the subject; the dummy auxiliary 'do' must be inserted.
rules.violation: A lexical (non-auxiliary) verb is directly followed by 'not', or is placed before its subject to form an interrogative, without 'do' or another auxiliary.

correct.text: Do you want to go with them?

incorrect.note: Lexical verb 'saw' followed directly by 'not'. Source pattern: p. 51 [3i].
Lexical verb inverted with subject. Source pattern: p. 51 [3ii].

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: auxiliary vs lexical verbs: not and inversion
burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Described for contemporary standard English; the page does not mention archaic or poetic uses ('I know not'). 'Be' counts as an auxiliary even as copula (WCAT-002), so it is not subject to this restriction.

rules.concept: be as auxiliary in copula use
rules.statement: Because auxiliaries are defined syntactically, be is an auxiliary verb even in its copula use, as in 'They are cheap', where it takes 'not' and inverts with the subject.
rules.condition: Applies to the verb be in any use (progressive, passive or copula): it takes a following 'not' and inverts with the subject to form interrogatives.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: be as auxiliary in copula use
burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Cambridge classes copular 'be' as an auxiliary, unlike traditional grammar's linking verb.

rules.statement: English has two tense systems: a primary one marked by verb inflection (preterite vs present) and a secondary one marked by the presence or absence of auxiliary have (perfect vs non-perfect); the two combine into compound tenses.
rules.condition: Applies when describing the tense of a verb phrase: primary tense is preterite or present (inflectional); secondary tense is perfect (have + past participle) or non-perfect; preterite perfect and present perfect are compound tenses.

correct.text: She is believed to have been ill. [perfect, secondary tense]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.concept: tense vs time; no future tense
rules.statement: Tense is a grammatical category and time a semantic one: a preterite form need not refer to past time, and since will and shall are modal auxiliaries, English has no future tense.
rules.condition: Applies when assigning tense: the tense category is determined by verb form (preterite vs present), not by the time referred to; will and shall are classed with must, may and can as modal auxiliaries and do not mark a tense.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: tense vs time; no future tense
burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Analytic claim that departs from traditional grammar. The engine must not flag 'will' as a 'missing tense'; and must not treat it as part of a tense paradigm.

rules.statement: Grammatical aspect is marked by the presence or absence of auxiliary be (progressive vs non-progressive); the meaning contrast of aspectuality is perfective vs imperfective, and the progressive mainly expresses a kind of imperfective.
rules.condition: Applies when describing progressive verb phrases: aspect (form) is progressive (be + gerund-participle) vs non-progressive; aspectuality (meaning) is perfective (situation viewed as a whole) vs imperfective (viewed from within).

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: Mood is a matter of grammatical form and modality of meaning; the main markers of mood in English are the modal auxiliaries can, may, must, will, shall (plus a few less central ones), and irrealis were is a residual mood form.
rules.condition: Applies when identifying modal auxiliaries: can, may, must, will and shall are central modals; modality (meaning) can be expressed by means other than modals.

correct.text: I wish he were here. [irrealis mood]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: 'A few less central ones' are not listed on this page; the list is open until Ch. 3 is processed.

rules.statement: Modal meaning is of three main kinds: deontic (obligation, permission, prohibition), epistemic (speaker's commitment to the truth of the proposition) and dynamic (properties and dispositions, esp. of the subject); all can also be expressed by lexical verbs, adjectives, adverbs and nouns.
rules.condition: Applies when interpreting modal expressions: deontic modality concerns obligation or permission, epistemic modality qualifies the speaker's commitment to truth, dynamic modality concerns the subject's properties or dispositions; non-auxiliary means of expression include lexical verbs, adjectives, adverbs and nouns.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: The same modal can carry different kinds of meaning in different sentences; the book flags 'central cases'. Do not use this as an error-detection rule.

rules.statement: Dependents of the verb in clause structure are either complements or modifiers; complements are more closely related to the verb, their presence depends on the verb's subclass, and the semantic role of a complement NP depends on the verb's meaning.
rules.condition: Applies when classifying a verb dependent in a clause: complements are licensed by the verb's subclass and linked closely to it; modifiers are less closely linked; the semantic role of the complement (e.g. patient, stimulus) varies with the verb.

correct.text: They met on Friday. [modifier: on Friday]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: Whether a canonical clause has an object depends on the verb's subclass: some verbs require an object (use), others exclude one (arrive).
rules.condition: Applies to canonical clauses headed by a verb whose subclass either requires an object (transitive, as with 'use') or excludes one (intransitive, as with 'arrive').
rules.violation: A verb that excludes an object is followed by an object NP, or a verb that requires an object in canonical clauses has none.

exceptions.description: Many verbs occur in more than one complementation: 'read' is intransitive, monotransitive or ditransitive depending on the clause.

incorrect.note: Object-requiring verb with no object (canonical clause).

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Verb-by-verb subclass lists belong to Ch. 4; this record only states the principle. Only canonical clauses are covered; non-canonical clauses may omit objects.

rules.statement: The subject is an external complement and is obligatory in every canonical clause.
rules.condition: Applies to canonical clauses (positive, declarative, active, main, non-coordinate): the subject is an obligatory element located outside the VP.
rules.violation: A canonical clause has no subject.

exceptions.description: Non-canonical clauses may lack an expressed subject, e.g. imperatives and VP-subordinator clauses ('to use') (the latter noted on p. 47).

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Applies only to canonical clauses; informal ellipsis ('Arrived late.') is non-canonical and is outside this source's claim. Engine must first decide that a clause is canonical.

rules.statement: The three major clause constructions are intransitive (subject + predicator), monotransitive (plus an object) and ditransitive (plus indirect and direct objects); the terms apply to the clause or to the head verb, and most verbs occur in more than one complementation.
rules.condition: Applies when classifying clauses by their object complements: no object, one object, or indirect plus direct objects; a given verb may appear in more than one of the three.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: Objects normally have the form of NPs; in 'gave the key to me' the 'to me' phrase is a PP complement, not an indirect object, although the meaning matches 'gave me the key'.
rules.condition: Applies to ditransitive alternations: 'me' in 'gave me the key' is an indirect object (NP form); 'to me' in 'gave the key to me' is a complement with PP form and is not an object.

correct.text: They gave me the key. [indirect object]
They gave the key to me. [PP complement, not an object]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Cambridge narrows 'object' to NP forms; traditional grammar calls the to-phrase an indirect object.

rules.statement: A predicative complement is an internal complement that can be realised by an adjective and typically ascribes a property to the subject (complex-intransitive) or object (complex-transitive); objects, by contrast, refer to participants.
rules.condition: Applies to clauses with verbs like seem, consider: complex-intransitive = subject + predicator + predicative complement; complex-transitive = subject + predicator + object + predicative complement.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: Be in complex-intransitive clauses is either ascriptive (the predicative gives a property of the subject) or specifying (it identifies the value of a variable); specifying clauses normally allow subject and predicative to be reversed.
rules.condition: Applies to clauses with be plus a predicative complement: ascriptive when the predicative ascribes a property to the subject; specifying when the clause identifies something; only the specifying type normally permits reversal of subject and predicative.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: Prepositional verbs take a PP complement headed by a preposition the verb selects (refer to, blame on/for); the selected preposition belongs in constituent structure with its NP, and with 'regard' and 'count' the complement of 'as' is predicative.
rules.condition: Applies to verbs that select a specific preposition for their PP complement: the preposition is part of the PP, not of the verb; in the 'as' constructions, the complement of 'as' is a predicative, not an object.

correct.text: They blamed the delay on Jon.
They blamed Jon for the delay.
He regards the plan as a risk.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Cambridge notes blame can select either on or for. This record lists only the verbs the page names.

rules.statement: A complement that is a PP consisting of a preposition alone can precede or follow the direct object; such complements are called particles, whereas in 'jumped off the wall' the VP has one PP complement.
rules.condition: Applies to clauses with 'off' or similar prepositions: with a particle the VP has two complements (the preposition and the direct object, in either order); with an ordinary preposition-plus-NP the VP has a single PP complement.

correct.text: She jumped off the wall. [one complement: PP]
She took off the label. [particle + object]
She took the label off. [object + particle]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: Prototypical NPs are headed by nouns and can function as complement; the main noun subcategories are common nouns, proper nouns and pronouns, and pronoun is a subcategory of noun, not a distinct part of speech.
rules.condition: Applies when classifying words heading NPs: common noun, proper noun and pronoun are all subcategories of noun.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Cambridge departs from the traditional part-of-speech list; Burton-Roberts's treatment not checked.

traditional_terms: pronoun as a part of speech

rules.statement: Determiner is a function in NP structure and determinative is a lexical category; determinatives are a distinct primary category (traditionally a subclass of adjectives) and can have functions other than determiner, while determiners may also be genitive NPs.
rules.condition: Applies to words like the, a, my, three, much: determinative is the category and determiner the NP-internal function marking definiteness; a determinative may instead function as modifier (e.g. in 'these three books'), and a genitive NP may be the determiner.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Cambridge's 'determinative' category contradicts the traditional treatment; compare with Burton-Roberts.

rules.review_notes: Flag for Burton-Roberts comparison: category inventory differs from traditional grammar.

rules.statement: Noun senses are either count (a dog; combine with cardinal numerals) or non-count (some equipment); certain determiners occur only or almost only with count nouns (a, each, every, either, several, many) and others with non-count nouns (much, little, a little).
rules.condition: Applies to the sense of a noun in context: a count sense can combine with one, two, three; a non-count sense cannot; determiner selection follows the count/non-count distinction.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: The book hedges ('only, or almost only'); this is descriptive and not an error rule. Classification is by noun sense, not by word.

rules.statement: An NP has a determiner and a head nominal; the hierarchy NP > nominal > noun parallels clause > VP > verb; modifiers and complements inside the nominal are internal dependents, while peripheral modifiers and predeterminers are external.
rules.condition: Applies to NP analysis: first split is determiner plus nominal; the nominal contains the head noun and its modifiers or complements (internal dependents); elements like 'quite' and 'all' attach to a whole NP (external dependents); the nominal level may be omitted when there is no modifier or complement.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: An attributive modifier is an internal pre-head dependent in a nominal; it is most often an adjective, but can also be a nominal, a determinative or a verb or VP in gerund-participle or past participle form.
rules.condition: Applies to modifiers before the head noun: adjectival (young), nominal (federal government inquiry), determinative (her many virtues) or verbal (a sleeping child; a frequently overlooked problem).

correct.text: a recently repaired road [VP, past participle]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: With very restricted exceptions, an attributive modifier before the head noun cannot itself contain a post-head dependent.
rules.condition: Applies to a pre-head attributive modifier in a nominal: it may be a simple adjective, nominal or verb form, but may not take its own dependents after it (such as a than-phrase or an adverb following the verb).
rules.violation: A pre-head attributive modifier is followed by its own post-head dependent (e.g. a than-phrase or a post-verbal adverb) before the head noun.

exceptions.description: The source says there are 'very restricted exceptions' but does not list them on this page; the statement 'with only very restricted exceptions' is recorded as is.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Exceptions unlisted here: check Ch. 5 / Ch. 6 before flagging examples with rare modifier patterns as errors.

rules.statement: Direct complements are licensed by the head of the nominal (his fear of the dark; the claim that it was a hoax); indirect complements are licensed by a dependent of the head (a better result than we'd expected; enough time to complete the work) and occur in most kinds of phrase.
rules.condition: Applies to complements in NPs: direct if licensed by the head noun; indirect if licensed by a dependent such as a comparative form or 'enough'.

correct.text: the claim that it was false [direct]
a worse result than we expected [indirect: licensed by 'worse']
enough money to buy the car [indirect: licensed by 'enough']

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: In some NPs the head is fused with a dependent, so one word functions as head and as determiner or modifier; words like 'any' and 'several' in such uses are determinatives, not pronouns.
rules.condition: Applies to NPs with no separate head noun where one word is both head and determiner (some, any, several) or head and modifier (the rich, the cheaper of the two).

correct.text: I need some pens but can't find any.
I chose the cheaper of the two.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Traditional grammar calls these pronouns; Cambridge says determinatives.

rules.concept: case forms of pronouns and nouns
rules.statement: A few pronouns have four case forms (we, us, our, ours); most nouns contrast only genitive and plain case, case is determined by the NP's function, and genitive is marked on the last word of the NP (head genitive or phrasal genitive).
rules.condition: Applies to case marking: nominative, accusative, dependent genitive and independent genitive for a few pronouns; plain vs genitive (dog vs dog's, dogs vs dogs') for most nouns; genitive marking falls on the last word, usually the head noun but sometimes on the last word of a post-head dependent.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: case forms of pronouns and nouns
burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: A genitive NP typically functions as subject-determiner in a larger NP, combining determiner and subject-complement functions; it can fuse with the head ('Mara's was better').
rules.condition: Applies to genitive NPs inside an NP: they mark the NP as definite and function as its subject; in 'the behaviour of the minister' the determiner and complement are realised separately; the genitive may be fused with the head when the head is omitted.

correct.text: the advice of the teacher [determiner 'the' + internal complement]
Your plan failed, but Mara's worked. [fused genitive]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: In an NP the number of the head noun must be compatible with the determinative: this and that agree with the head, and other determinatives select either a singular head (a, each) or a plural head (two, several).
rules.condition: Applies to NPs with a determiner that is a determinative: singular-selecting determinatives (a, each, this, that) combine with a singular count head; plural-selecting determinatives (two, several, these, those) combine with a plural head.
rules.violation: A singular-selecting determinative is followed by a plural head noun, or a plural-selecting determinative by a singular count head noun.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: The page names a, each, two, several; the rest of the determinatives are in Ch. 5. Non-count heads (e.g. 'much equipment') are outside this record. Compound modifiers ('a two-week trip') are not considered.

rules.statement: A verb in the present tense (and be in the preterite) agrees in person and number with its subject NP, whose person-number classification normally derives from its head noun.
rules.condition: Applies to finite clauses with a present-tense verb (or preterite be) and a subject NP: the verb's form matches the subject's person and number as determined by the head noun of the NP.
rules.violation: The verb's number or person form does not match the person and number of the subject NP (as derived from its head noun, subject to the listed departures).

exceptions.description: Subjects whose notional number differs from the head noun's form: 'A number of boys were absent' (singular head, plural subject) and 'Three eggs is plenty' (plural head, single-quantity subject). The source says there are 'a good few' such departures.

correct.text: A number of players were injured.
correct.note: Head 'number' is singular but the subject counts as plural.
Plural head, but the subject expresses one quantity.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Applies to the standard variety; non-standard agreement patterns are not discussed here. The full treatment of agreement departures is in later chapters (not supplied here); check before engine use.

rules.concept: singular count nouns need a determiner
rules.statement: A singular count noun cannot in general head an NP without a determiner.
rules.condition: Applies to NPs whose head is a singular noun in a count sense: such an NP needs a determiner (the, a, your, ...).
rules.violation: A singular count noun heads a subject or complement NP with no determiner.

exceptions.description: The source says 'in general', so exceptions exist but are not listed on this page.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: singular count nouns need a determiner
burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Hedged by the source ('in general'). Do not flag cases like bare plurals, non-count nouns or proper nouns: those are outside the rule's scope; unlisted exceptions with count nouns need Ch. 5.

conflicts.description: These records reflect Cambridge's departures from traditional grammar (auxiliary as head, determinative category, pronoun as noun, copula be as auxiliary, no future tense, narrower 'object'). Burton-Roberts's treatment not supplied; may differ.
conflicts.proposed_resolution: Compare against Burton-Roberts chapter notes before approval; keep both analyses with a mapping if they differ.
